name: Bakole
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Ewote, James 1973. The phonology of Kole (Glottolog ref 587014; not online). Also Asobo 1989 The Noun Class System of Kole (MPI pure handle returns 403).

new_statements.quote: The kɔlɛ language makes use of four level tones. These tones are H (high), L (low), LH (low-high rising tone), HL (high-low falling tone).
new_statements.citation: Asobo, Irene Swiri. 1989. The Noun Class System of Kɔlɛ. Post-graduate diploma (Maîtrise) dissertation, Université de Yaoundé. §2.1.4 'Tones' (numbered 2.4 in the table of contents), p. 23; tone-pattern examples continue on p. 24.
new_statements.locator: p. 23 (PDF page 29 of 131), §2.1.4 Tones; examples p. 24 (PDF p. 30). Quote checked against the page image; the text layer (Acrobat Capture scanned) renders kɔlɛ as 'kale'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for stress: the only accessible description presents Kɔlɛ as a tone language with two level tones (H, L) and two contour tones (LH, HL) contrasting on nouns, and never mentions word stress, accent or prominence. Nothing can be said about where stress falls; the source is silent on it rather than denying it.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the section is a two-page résumé of the tonal system, explicitly based on Ewota 1973 (p. 16).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: citation forms of nouns (mono-, di- and trisyllabic) in isolation, e.g. kɔ́ 'snail', mbɔ̀ 'honey', dìbé 'breast', mbɔ́à 'village', kárárá 'corn', mɔ̀kɔ́kɔ́ 'sugarcane', ìréndè 'knife' (p. 24). Vowel length is said to be non-phonemic (p. 16); syllable structure (C)V(C), predominantly open CV (pp. 21-22). Noun-class prefixes are stated to be always low-toned ('The tone for the noun prefixes are always low', concord chapter).
new_statements.identity_note: Asobo 1989 describes the Kɔlɛ (Kole) spoken in the six fishing settlements around Bamusso (Bekanje, Ubenikang, Betika, Njangasa, Bekumu, Yenda, Bamusso), Ndian division, SW Cameroon, ~400 speakers in 1989; identified by the author with ALCAM no. 625 'bakole' and with Guthrie A.20 (Duala-Limbe group). This is Glottolog bako1250 / ISO kme itself, not a differently named variety. Note that English Wikipedia redirects 'Bakole language' to Kpwe (Mokpwe, bri, mokp1239), calling Kole mutually intelligible with Kpwe; Glottolog and ISO keep it a separate language, and Asobo's data were collected from Kole speakers. Ebobissé 2014 treats Kole (KOL) as one of the Sawabantu lects.

Chapter 2 'General phonology of Kɔlɛ' (pp. 16-24: vowels, consonants, syllable and morpheme structure, tones) is a sketch avowedly based on Ewota's 1973 phonology; §2.1.4 'Tones' (pp. 23-24) states the language has four tones H, L, LH (rising), HL (falling) and lists tone patterns on mono-, di- and trisyllabic nouns. The words 'stress', 'accent', 'prominence', 'pitch-accent' do not occur anywhere in the text layer except in the non-technical phrase 'important to stress here' (p. 12). sources.citation: English Wikipedia, 'Kpwe language' (to which 'Bakole language' redirects), citing Atindogbé 2013, A grammatical sketch of Mòkpè (Bakweri), African Study Monographs Suppl. 45: 5-163.
sources.note: Treats Kole as mutually intelligible with Kpwe; gives a five-tone system for Kpwe (high, downstepped high, low, rising, falling) and says nothing about stress or about Kole specifically. Not a Bakole source.
Segment inventory only, derived from Asobo 1989; no prosodic statement. Confirms Asobo 1989 is the only phonological source in the database for this language.

sources.note: Only the DNB-digitised table of contents was obtainable (image PDF, scanned to). Kapitel 2 'Phonologie' has, for each of three subgroups (Zentral-, Süd-, Südwestgruppe), sections Konsonanten / Gleitlaute / Vokale / Toneme / Bemerkungen, then 'Regelmäßige Tonentsprechungen' and 'Silbenstrukturen'. sources.note: The only descriptive items for Bakole are Ewota 1973 (phonology), Asobo 1989 (grammar sketch) and Ebobissé 2014 (comparative overview/wordlist); the rest are sociolinguistic/endangerment surveys (Connell 2007, Sommer 1992, Moseley 2010) and Ardener 1956 (ethnographic overview). The kole1239 list adds only Isubu/Wovea material (Mokake 2021 reference grammar of Isubu, Sirih-Nagang 2020, Merrick 1854, Saker 1852) which concerns the sister language szv, not Bakole.
